title: Introduce duplicate message processing
description: Project: Introduce duplicate message processing. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Message queues promise at-least-once delivery, which means consumers must handle duplicates gracefully. Without idempotency, a retried message or a redelivered event can create duplicate charges, double bookings, or corrupt aggregates. This lesson covers the duplicate-message problem, idempotency key design, and deduplication strategies at the consumer level.

items: Consumer crashes after processing but before acknowledging the message
Network partition causes the broker to redeliver unacknowledged messages
Consumer group rebalance causes partitions to be reassigned and offsets to reset
Manual retries in the application layer without tracking processed message IDs
Poison messages that fail repeatedly and are eventually retried after TTL expiry

terms.definition: A unique identifier included in a message that the consumer uses to detect and skip duplicate processing.
A messaging guarantee where each message is delivered and processed exactly once, regardless of retries or failures.
A queue where messages are routed after repeated processing failures, allowing operators to inspect and replay them manually.
A message that consistently causes consumer failures due to bad data or serialization errors.
The time period during which a consumer should remember processed message IDs to reject duplicates.

data.text: Idempotency is most critical on write operations. Reading the same message twice is harmless; charging a customer twice is not. Design your consumer so that reprocessing produces the same result as processing once. The easiest way is to make every handler a pure function of the idempotency key and the message payload.

data.title: Idempotent message handler with Redis deduplication
data.content: A background service that checks a deduplication store before processing:

items: Use the message ID as a deduplication key stored in Redis or a database with TTL
Leverage broker-native deduplication where available, such as Kafka idempotent producers
Use database unique constraints on business keys as the final guard against duplicates
Design handlers so reprocessing is safe even when the deduplication store is cold
Route poison messages to a dead-letter queue after a configurable retry limit

cards.title: At-least-once with dedup
cards.description: Broker may redeliver; consumer must handle duplicates.

cards.title: Exactly-once (Kafka)
cards.description: Broker and consumer cooperate to process each message once.

cards.title: At-most-once
cards.description: Messages may be dropped but never duplicated.
cons: Not suitable for financial or audit events

data.caption: Message processing flow with idempotency check
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Message received] --> B{Check dedup store}
    B -->|Found| C[Skip and ack]
    B -->|Not found| D[Process message]
    D --> E{Processing succeeded?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Write result]
    F --> G[Store dedup key with TTL]

    I --> J[Retry or DLQ]

    J --> K

data.title: Deduplication stores can fail too
data.text: If the deduplication store is unavailable, the consumer must choose between blocking or processing. Blocking preserves dedup guarantees but reduces throughput. Processing preserves throughput but risks duplicates. Document this trade-off explicitly and choose based on the business impact of duplicates.

items.question: How long should the deduplication window be?
items.answer: Long enough to exceed the maximum redelivery delay for your broker. For RabbitMQ with TTL, 24 hours is a common choice. For Kafka, the window should cover the maximum log retention period plus processing delay.

items.question: Do I need deduplication if I use a transaction?
items.answer: Database transactions prevent partial writes but do not prevent duplicate messages from being processed. A transaction can succeed twice on two redeliveries if the consumer does not track message IDs. Use transactions for atomicity and dedup for idempotency.

items.question: Can I rely on the broker for deduplication?
items.answer: Some brokers offer idempotent consumers or deduplication plugins. These are helpful but should be treated as an additional layer, not a replacement for application-level idempotency. Broker behavior can change across versions or during failover.

data.title: Add idempotency to a payment processor
data.description: Your payment processor consumes events from a queue and charges customers. A retried event has already charged some customers twice. Design the idempotency mechanism and describe how you would recover from the duplicate charges already made.
steps: Identify the business key for each payment event
Design the idempotency key and where to store it
Define the recovery process for already-duplicated charges
Add monitoring for duplicate detection rate
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce an idempotent consumer design with a rollback plan and observability for duplicate detection.

data.title: Summary
points: At-least-once delivery means duplicates are inevitable; design for them
Idempotency keys with TTL-based dedup stores are the standard defense
Database unique constraints are the final guard against duplicates
Poison messages need a dead-letter path, not infinite retries
Test dedup behavior by replaying the same message twice
data.takeaway: A senior engineer assumes every message will be delivered more than once and builds the consumer so that reprocessing is harmless. This assumption is the difference between a system that survives failures and one that silently corrupts data.
